# The offline default build

A plain `cargo build` or `cargo test` at the root of this workspace **links no
HTTP client**. Not "does not make requests" — does not *contain* one. No
`reqwest`, no chain RPC client, no processor SDK, no signing library for a
chain you are not using.

That is deliberate, it is load-bearing, and it is held up by two different
mechanisms which are worth understanding separately because they are used for
different reasons.

## Why it matters

- **CI needs no chain and no processor.** A test run that cannot reach a
  network cannot be flaky because of one, and cannot quietly start depending
  on one.
- **A default build cannot leak.** If the code to make an outbound request is
  not linked, no amount of misconfiguration turns a unit test into a live
  call. This is a structural guarantee, not a policy someone has to remember.
- **The blast radius of a supply-chain problem tracks what you compiled in.**
  A consumer who needs only the currency table and an offline manual rail
  should not inherit a TLS stack, and here does not.
- **You can read the tree.** `cargo tree` is a short list rather than a wall,
  which makes an unexpected dependency visible instead of buried.

`PATALA.md` §8 states it as a binding convention: *"Default build stays
offline: no new mandatory deps, no network, CI needs no chain or processor."*

## Mechanism 1 — `default-members` excludes the crypto and Hyperswitch rails

`patala-solana`, `patala-stellar` and `patala-hyperswitch` are real workspace
members, but they are deliberately left **out of `default-members`**:

```toml
[workspace]
members = [
    "patala-core", "patala-uniffi", "patala-ffi", "patala-py", "patala-sidecar",
    "patala-solana", "patala-stellar", "patala-hyperswitch", "patala-fiat",
]
default-members = ["patala-core", "patala-uniffi", "patala-ffi", "patala-py", "patala-sidecar", "patala-fiat"]
```

So a bare `cargo build` / `cargo test` at the root never builds them. Reaching
them is explicit and per-crate:

```bash
cargo build -p patala-solana
cargo test  -p patala-stellar
```

These three carry real network and crypto dependencies on purpose —
`reqwest`, `ed25519-dalek`, `curve25519-dalek`, `stellar-xdr`,
`stellar-strkey`, `hmac`, `sha2`, `bs58`. Nothing about that is accidental or
regrettable; a chain rail that does not talk to a chain would be useless. The
decision is only about **who pays for it**, and the answer is: whoever asks
for that rail by name.

## Mechanism 2 — `patala-fiat` stays in, and gates its deps behind features

`patala-fiat` uses the opposite trick, because it has a genuinely useful
offline half. Its `default` feature set is **empty**, and each of the twenty
processor adapters is its own Cargo feature pulling in only what that adapter
needs:

```toml
# The currency table, the registry and the offline `manual` rail. No network stack.
patala-fiat = { path = "../patala-fiat" }

# One processor, and only that processor's dependencies.
patala-fiat = { path = "../patala-fiat", features = ["stripe"] }
```

So it can stay *in* `default-members` — `cargo build` at the root compiles the
ISO-4217 currency table, the provider registry and the always-available
`manual` rail, and still links no HTTP client — while
`cargo test -p patala-fiat --all-features` exercises the Stripe and Paystack
pilots against `wiremock`.

Two mechanisms rather than one, because the crates differ: a chain rail is
useless without its network stack, and a fiat crate has a large, valuable,
genuinely offline core.

## The evidence

Measured in this checkout, with `cargo tree -e normal` (normal dependencies
only — no dev-dependencies, no build-dependencies), counting **unique crates**:

| What you build | Unique crates | `reqwest`? |
|---|---|---|
| Default workspace build (`cargo tree -e normal`) | **123** | **no — 0 matches** |
| `patala-core` alone | 12 | no |
| `patala-fiat`, default features | 17 | no |
| `patala-fiat --all-features` (20 adapters) | **103** | yes |
| `patala-solana` | 114 | yes |
| `patala-stellar` | 112 | yes |
| `patala-hyperswitch` | 101 | yes |
| `patala-sidecar` | 69 | no |
| `patala-py`, default features | 76 | no |

Reproduce any row:

```bash
cargo tree -e normal | grep -c reqwest            # 0
cargo tree -p patala-fiat -e normal --depth 1     # 5 direct deps, none of them HTTP
cargo tree -p patala-fiat -e normal --all-features | grep -c reqwest
```

`patala-fiat` going from **17 crates to 103** when every adapter is compiled
in is the whole argument in one number. That is what the default build is not
paying for.

### One honest correction

`hyper` **is** in the default workspace tree. It arrives through `axum`, which
is what `patala-sidecar` is built on — the sidecar is an HTTP *server*, so a
server stack in its dependency tree is the thing itself, not a leak:

```text
$ cargo tree -i hyper -e normal
hyper v1.11.0
├── axum v0.7.9
│   └── patala-sidecar v0.1.2
└── hyper-util v0.1.20
    └── axum v0.7.9 (*)
```

`-e normal` is doing real work in that command: without it the tree also shows
`reqwest` and `wiremock` arriving as **dev-dependencies**, which are not in a
build and would make the paragraph above look wrong when it is right.

The precise claim is the one worth making: **the default build contains no
outbound HTTP client and no chain or processor code.** Saying "no HTTP
anything" would be neater and would be false, and a claim that is slightly
false is worse than one that is exactly true.

## What enforces this

Structure alone is not a gate — a crate can be added to `default-members` in a
one-line diff that reviews cleanly. What actually holds the property:

- **`make check` runs seven gates** — `fmt-check`, `lint`, `test`,
  `test-features`, `doc`, `features` and `site-check` — and the two test passes
  are both of them, not one. `cargo test --workspace` uses each crate's
  *default* feature set, and `patala-fiat`'s is empty, so a plain `--workspace`
  run executes the currency table, the registry and the `manual` rail and
  **none** of the twenty adapters. That was hundreds of tests that existed and
  never ran. `make test-features` is the fix, and it is part of `check`, not an
  optional extra:

  ```make
  test:
  	cargo test --workspace
  test-features:
  	cargo test -p patala-fiat --all-features
  	cargo test -p patala-uniffi --features fiat-all
  	cargo test -p patala-ffi --features fiat-all
  ```

- **Clippy is run twice for the same reason.** `cargo clippy --workspace`
  lints each crate with its default features, which for `patala-fiat` means
  twenty adapters never linted at all. The second invocation
  (`-p patala-fiat --all-features`) is not redundant.

- **`scripts/check-features.sh`** keeps the adapter set in lock-step with the
  Cargo features that expose it. A new `patala-fiat` adapter left out of
  `patala-uniffi`'s `fiat-all` would compile fine and silently vanish from the Go
  binding's cdylib — present in Rust, absent in every other language, with
  nothing failing. That script fails the build instead.

  **It also builds and lints all twenty processor features individually**, which
  is new in 0.1.1 and is what makes the promise on this page true. Until then
  **fourteen of the twenty single-processor builds did not compile at all**:
  `src/httpshared.rs` gated itself on six feature names while fifteen adapters
  called into it. `--all-features` and the empty default set both compiled, so
  nothing in `make check` ever built the one-processor configuration this page
  recommends, and the only workaround was `--all-features` — twenty processors
  linked into a payments binary, the exact outcome the design exists to avoid.
  The `features = ["stripe"]` example above happened to be one of the six that
  worked.

## What this costs you

Stated plainly, so the trade is visible:

- **You have to opt in per rail**, and you will forget once. The symptom is a
  constructor that does not exist in your build; see
  [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md).
- **`cargo test --workspace` is not the whole suite.** Run `make check`, not
  `cargo test`, or you are running roughly a third of it.
- **Bindings inherit the same rule.** `PatalaRail.new_fiat` and
  `PatalaRailNewFiat` only exist in bindings generated from a cdylib built
  with the fiat features. A plain `cargo build -p patala-uniffi` does not include
  them, and that is not a bug.
